# Abstract

This settlement gazetteer compiles urban, town and oasis population records for 1.200 catalogued archaeological sites across Anatolia, Cyprus, the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula between 3200BC and 539BC. Selected from 1.450 candidate records after removing 250 duplicate, uncertain or non-residential monuments, the corpus spans fourteen modern jurisdictions from Turkey (617 sites) and Syria (176 sites) to Israel (171), Cyprus (65), Oman (61), Jordan (43), Saudi Arabia (20), Lebanon (16) and Yemen (14). Because settlement across this 3,62M km² domain grew upon rain-fed Mediterranean plains, intermontane basins, monsoon-fed Yemeni highlands and coastal copper-trading harbours rather than a single river alluvium, the urban hierarchy exhibits a flat rank-size slope ($\alpha = 0{,}398$, $R^2 = 0{,}671$). Leading towns cluster between 6k and 18k inhabitants, anchored by Tarsus, Palmyra, Tripolis, Byzantion, Kerkenes, Phocaea, Cnidus and Aphrodisias in the Iron Age alongside enduring Bronze Age hubs such as Byblos, Ashqelon, Idalion, Troy, Bat and Al-Khasbah.

# Background

Urban life across Ancient Anatolia, the Levant, Cyprus and Arabia emerged along very different lines from the centralised temple-palace cities of riverine lowlands. Here, no single navigable flood artery bound hundreds of thousands of farmers into one administrative hierarchy. Instead, walled towns rose wherever reliable winter rainfall, perennial limestone springs, metal ores or strategic caravan passes permitted surplus accumulation [@Massa2017Change; @Massa2020Landscape]. In Early Bronze Age Anatolia, citadels at Troy, Beycesultan and Alişar Höyük controlled modest valley territories, before Middle Bronze Age long-distance merchants established an Assyrian trading quarter outside the walls of Kültepe-Kanesh [@Ghazaryan2022Administra; @Kaderli2024Evaluation; @Veenhof2008Mesopotami]. Across Syria and the coastal Levant, third- and second-millennium centres such as Ebla, Tell Tayinat, Ugarit and Byblos flourished on rain-fed wheat, cedar timber and maritime exchange [@Manning2020Beyond; @Gimenez2021Toponym]. Further south, Bronze Age copper extraction at Bat, Al-Khasbah and Salut sustained fortified towers in Oman, while the first millennium BC witnessed the rise of Sabaean, Minaean, Qatabanian and Hadhrami oasis cities linked by camel caravans across the Hijaz [@EfratKowalsky2022Text].

# Methodology

The 1.200 included settlements in this gazetteer were assembled by harmonising the Published Excavations Atlas (709 matched sites), the Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer (640 matched sites), the Near East Radiocarbon Database (49 chronometric matches) and the C-Turkey Chronometric Register (11 Anatolian radiocarbon sites). Every coordinate pair was checked against smooth sub-regional vector masks and geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] to ensure exact geographic placement without coastal misregistration on Aegean islands, Cyprus or Bahrain. Where excavated architectural plans or lower-town mound surveys record occupied hectares, resident population is estimated using regional density benchmarks (100 to 180 persons per hectare in compact tell cities; 40 to 80 persons per hectare in dispersed highland and oasis settlements) [@Palmisano2017Confrontin; @Osborne2020City]. Where only multi-period site class and horizon continuity exist, estimates are scaled to sub-regional totals and tested against Zipf rank-size diagnostics before radial Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging projects background rural density across surrounding catchments.

# Testing and Validation

Temporal density across the 1.200 sites confirms robust multi-millennial continuity rather than modern survey bias concentrated solely in the Classical period. At 3200BC, 484 sites carry active population estimates; by 3000BC and 2500BC, 805 sites are active; by 2000BC, 826 sites; by 1500BC, 854 sites; by 1000BC, 909 sites; and by 539BC, 1.160 sites. Figure 2 displays the rank-size regression across the entire catalogued sample alongside the twelve highest-peaking sites. Because this 1.200-settlement corpus comfortably exceeds minimum sample thresholds, the estimated Zipf slope ($\alpha = 0{,}398$, $R^2 = 0{,}671$) reflects genuine polycentric urban dispersion rather than sampling truncation: maritime ports, Anatolian plateau fortresses, Levantine highland capitals and Arabian caravan oases shared demographic weight across dozens of rival polities rather than concentrating inside one imperial metropolis.

# Results

## Western, Southern and Central Anatolia

Turkey accounts for 617 of the 1.200 settlements in this chapter, reflecting both dense Bronze and Iron Age mound landscapes and intensive archaeological survey across the Aegean littoral, Cilicia, the Konya plain and the Kızılırmak bend [@Massa2020Landscape; @Ross2019Anatolian]. Table 1 lists the twenty-five largest Anatolian centres by peak pre-539BC population. Along the western and southern coasts, Ionian, Carian and Cilician ports such as Tarsus (17,3k), Byzantion/Constantinopolis (16,1k), Phocaea (14,2k), Cnidus (14,2k) and Aphrodisias (13,8k) expanded rapidly during the first millennium BC, joined by inland Phrygian and Luwian strongholds including Kerkenes (15,9k), Ilium/Troia (6,5k), Fırakdın (6,5k), Šinuhtu (6,5k) and the Early-to-Middle Bronze Age tin-mining and trade centres at Göltepe and Kültepe [@Fairbairn2018Ceremonial; @KORKMAZ2021Modern].

## Cyprus

Cyprus (Alashiya) contributes 65 catalogued sites across its coastal plains, Mesaoria basin and Troodos copper foothills. Table 2 presents the twenty largest Cypriot settlements. Unlike the continental Anatolian interior, Cypriot urbanism pivoted around copper metallurgy and eastern Mediterranean maritime access from the Late Bronze Age through the Archaic city-kingdoms [@Kelder2022Thutmose]. Sites such as Pyla-Kokkinokremos, Marion, Idalion, Kissonerga-Skalia, Pigades, Enkomi and Kition regularly reached 4k to 6,5k inhabitants, forming a remarkably dense island network along the southern and eastern bays.

## Northern Levant: Syria and Phoenicia

Syria (176 sites) and Lebanon (16 sites) together form the Northern Levant corridor linking the upper Euphrates and Orontes valleys to the Phoenician ports. Table 3 displays the twenty-five largest Northern Levantine centres. Inland, Palmyra (17,1k), Antiochia/Orontes precursors (17,3k), Umm el-Marra (6,5k), Til-Bašerê (6,5k), Aleppo and Tell Tayinat anchored rain-fed grain plains and caravan crossings [@Manning2020Beyond; @Gimenez2021Toponym; @Warbinek2023Theonyms]. On the narrow Mediterranean littoral, Tripolis (16,5k), Byblos (6,5k), Sidon (6,4k), Beirut (6,4k), Chhim (6,3k) and Tyre drove maritime timber and silver trade across the Mediterranean [@Eshel2024Thousand; @Koiv2022Monarchy].

## Southern Levant: Israel, Palestine and Jordan

The Southern Levant contributes 220 catalogued sites across Israel (171), Jordan (43) and Palestine (6). Table 4 lists the twenty-five highest-peaking settlements across the coastal plain, Galilean and Judaean highlands and Transjordanian plateau. Early Bronze and Canaanite cities such as Tel Bet Yerah, Tell es-Sakan and Ashqelon (each peaking around 6,5k) were joined in the Iron Age by fortified administrative towns including Tell en-Nasbeh, Sahab, Amman, Characmoba, Zodacatha and Tananir [@Dziadosz2023Covenants; @Routledge2017There].

## Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf

Across the Arabian Peninsula and Gulf littoral, 106 catalogued sites span Oman (61), Saudi Arabia (20), Yemen (14), Bahrain (4), the United Arab Emirates (4), Kuwait (2) and Qatar (1). Table 5 records the twenty-five largest Arabian and Gulf centres. In Oman and the Gulf, Bronze Age copper and trade hubs at Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn (6,5k), Al-Khasbah (6,5k), Salut (6,5k), Saar on Bahrain (6,5k), ed-Dur (6,4k) and Failaka (5,1k) formed the maritime backbone of Dilmun and Magan. Across Yemen and western Arabia, Sabaean and caravan oases including Ṣaʿda (5,8k), Ṣanʿāʾ (5,8k), Adane (5,8k), Khief al-Zarah (6,5k), Iathrippa (5,8k) and Macoraba (5,8k) linked monsoon-terraced agriculture to the Mediterranean incense markets [@EfratKowalsky2022Text].

# Limitations

Three gazetteer constraints merit explicit caution when interpreting individual site rows. First, several top-ranked Anatolian and Levantine entries derived from classical archaeological gazetteers reflect sixth-century BC Archaic urban circuits (such as Phocaea, Cnidus, Kerkenes and Feride Gül Tarla) whose earlier Bronze Age layers remain buried or unquantified, producing single-horizon 539BC entries rather than full continuous curves. Second, where regional surveys record fortified stone circuits without full interior excavation, uniform residential multipliers smooth over intramural gardens, shrines and granary courtyards [@Palmisano2017Confrontin; @Burgin2016Aspects]. Third, settlement recovery in Yemen and interior Saudi Arabia lags behind Turkey, Israel and Oman due to modern fieldwork access, leaving rural highland hamlets under-enumerated in the point ledger relative to continuous sub-regional totals.

# Conclusion

Taken together, the 1.200 settlements catalogued in this gazetteer confirm that Bronze and Iron Age urbanisation from the Aegean coast to the Indian Ocean followed a decentralised, polycentric pattern rather than a riverine primate hierarchy. Across fourteen modern countries, medium-sized towns of 3k to 18k inhabitants clustered along rain-fed Anatolian and Levantine plains, Cypriot copper valleys, Gulf trading bays and terraced Yemeni uplands. By anchoring coordinate-exact town trajectories to calibrated radiocarbon chronologies and geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries], this dataset provides the archaeological urban skeleton beneath the continuous 5-arcminute demographic surfaces from 3200BC to 539BC.
